title: Uses of Earth Materials
seo_title: Grade 11 General Science: Uses of Earth Materials Worksheets (Strengthened SHS)
standard_code: Grade 11 General Science, Term 3: Earth and space science
standard_text: Uses of Earth materials by people: minerals and ores, rocks and soils, water resources and energy resources; mining and quarrying; renewable and non-renewable resources and their sustainable use. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, General Science, Term 3)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 General Science worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Term 3): minerals and ores, rocks and soil, energy resources, mining and sustainable use. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: An ore is a rock from which a metal can be extracted at a profit.
key_sub: Non-renewable resources are used faster than they form.
body_html:
How to think about it

People use minerals and rocks for metals (gold, copper, nickel), construction (limestone for cement, sand and gravel), and everyday products. Soil is a resource for farming. The Philippines is a major producer of nickel and has rich gold and copper deposits.

Fossil fuels, minerals and soil form very slowly, so they are non-renewable on a human timescale. Mining brings jobs and products but can cause deforestation, erosion and water pollution; responsible mining, recycling and rehabilitation reduce the harm.

Example

Which rock is used to make cement?

Calcium carbonate

Answer: limestone

Example

Is soil renewable on a human timescale?

It forms slowly.

Answer: not really; it forms very slowly

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all rocks with metal are ores.
  • Thinking mining has no environmental cost.
  • Thinking resources will never run out.

items.q: How does bauxite form?
c: intense weathering in a hot, wet climate leaches other minerals and leaves aluminum oxides
items.e: It is a residual deposit.

items.q: When is open-cut mining used rather than underground mining?
c: when the ore is large and close to the surface
when the ore is very deep and narrow
items.e: The Super Pit at Kalgoorlie is open-cut.

items.q: Arnel asks how iron ore formed. What is the best explanation?
c: from seawater evaporating in shallow basins long ago
from hot, mineral-rich water and magma near volcanoes and plate boundaries
from iron that settled out of ancient oceans in layers
from plants from ancient swamps buried and squeezed for millions of years
items.e: Iron ore formed from iron that settled out of ancient oceans in layers.

items.q: Which method is used to explore for ore bodies by measuring small differences in gravity or magnetism?
items.e: Drilling then confirms the ore.

items.q: Rafael asks how copper and gold ores formed. What is the best explanation?
c: from hot, mineral-rich water and magma near volcanoes and plate boundaries
from plants from ancient swamps buried and squeezed for millions of years
from iron that settled out of ancient oceans in layers
from seawater evaporating in shallow basins long ago
items.e: Copper and gold ores formed from hot, mineral-rich water and magma near volcanoes and plate boundaries.

items.q: How did the rock of Kata Tjuta form?
c: from sand and gravel eroded from ancient mountains, then pressed and cemented
from mudstone changed by heat and pressure
from rounded pebbles and boulders cemented together
from lava that cooled slowly and cracked into columns
items.e: Kata Tjuta is conglomerate (sedimentary).

items.q: Isabel reads about a resource that formed from iron that settled out of ancient oceans in layers. Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how iron ore formed.

items.q: Jasmine reads about a resource that formed from tiny marine organisms buried in ocean sediments, then heated and pressed for millions of years. Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how oil and natural gas formed.

items.q: How did the rock of the Organ Pipes in Victoria form?
c: from layers of river sand pressed together
from rounded pebbles and boulders cemented together
from lava that cooled slowly and cracked into columns
from magma that cooled slowly deep underground
items.e: The Organ Pipes in Victoria is basalt (igneous).

items.q: How do oil and natural gas form?
c: remains of marine plankton are buried, heated and changed into hydrocarbons, which collect in traps
items.e: They need a source rock, reservoir rock and cap rock.

items.q: What kind of rock is Kata Tjuta made of?
items.e: It formed from rounded pebbles and boulders cemented together.

items.q: Why is a cap rock needed for an oil or gas reservoir?
c: it is impermeable, so it stops the oil and gas escaping upwards
items.e: Shale and salt are common cap rocks.

items.q: Why are fossil fuels called non-renewable?
c: they are found only in deserts
they form over millions of years, far slower than we use them
items.e: Coal, oil and gas are non-renewable.

items.q: Trisha reads about a resource that formed from hot, mineral-rich water and magma near volcanoes and plate boundaries. Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how copper and gold ores formed.

items.q: What is mineral processing (beneficiation)?
c: crushing ore and separating the valuable mineral from the waste rock
items.e: Flotation separates many sulfide minerals.

items.q: Patricia asks how coal formed. What is the best explanation?
c: from plants from ancient swamps buried and squeezed for millions of years
from hot, mineral-rich water and magma near volcanoes and plate boundaries
from iron that settled out of ancient oceans in layers
from tiny marine organisms buried in ocean sediments, then heated and pressed for millions of years
items.e: Coal formed from plants from ancient swamps buried and squeezed for millions of years.

items.q: What is a placer deposit?
c: heavy minerals such as gold concentrated by flowing water in river or beach sands
items.e: The 1,850s Victorian gold rush was mostly placer gold.

items.q: Rose reads about a resource that formed from seawater evaporating in shallow basins long ago. Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how rock salt formed.

items.q: What is an ore?
c: a pure metal found in nature
rock containing a mineral in high enough concentration to be mined at a profit
items.e: Whether a deposit is ore depends on price and cost.

items.q: Why can a deposit that was not ore become ore?
c: the metal grows in the rock
a rise in metal price or a cheaper mining method makes it profitable
the deposit moves closer to the surface
items.e: Economics defines ore.

items.q: What type of rock is marble?

items.q: Which rock is marble made from when it is changed by heat and pressure?

items.q: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
c: Weathering breaks rock down where it is; erosion carries the pieces away.
items.e: Then deposition.

items.q: Mudstone or shale is heated and squeezed deep underground without melting. Which rock forms?
items.e: Metamorphism.

items.q: How does sediment become sedimentary rock?
c: It is heated until it glows.
Layers are squashed (compaction) and stuck together (cementation).
items.e: Over millions of years.

items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: How do metamorphic rocks form?

items.q: Which kind of rock forms from layers of sand and mud pressed together?

items.q: Which of these is man-made, not a natural rock: a plastic toy rock, granite, marble or slate?
items.e: Bricks, concrete and glass are made by people; rocks form naturally.

items.q: Which of these is a natural rock: a brick, a china mug, a lump of limestone or tarmac?
items.e: Natural rocks form in the Earth over a very long time.

items.q: Which of these is a natural rock: concrete, glass, granite or tarmac?
items.e: Natural rocks form in the Earth over a very long time.

items.q: Which rock floats on water because it is full of gas bubbles?
items.e: Pumice forms from frothy lava.

items.q: Why is slate used for roof tiles?
c: It can be carved and polished to look beautiful.
It is rough and full of tiny holes.
It is very hard and does not wear away.
It is waterproof and splits into thin, flat sheets.
items.e: Rocks are chosen for their properties.

items.q: A rock has shiny crystals you can see. Which type is it most likely to be?
items.e: Slow cooling makes big crystals.

items.q: Why must mines be cleaned up after they close?
c: to stop erosion of the Moon
to protect water, soil and wildlife from pollution
items.e: Mining can harm the environment.

What is sustainable yield?
c: the amount of a resource that can be taken without reducing its long-term availability
the maximum amount that can be taken at once
the total amount of a resource
items.e: Used for fisheries, forests and water.

a plan to drain the rivers
a plan for mining in the basin

Which natural factor best explains this? People abandoned farms and migrated to other regions.
c: Rising sea level and stronger storm surges.
Long droughts that dried up farmland.
Frequent volcanic ash that weathers into fertile soil.
A large aquifer under dry plains.
items.e: Match the human activity to the natural factor.

items.q: An ore body contains 2000 tonnes of ore with a grade of 5% lead. How many tonnes of lead does it contain?
items.e: Mass of metal = 2000 × 5 ÷ 100 = 100 t.

items.q: A gold ore has a grade of 8 g per tonne. How many tonnes of ore must be processed to obtain 62.2 g of gold?
items.e: Ore = gold ÷ grade = 62.2 ÷ 8 = 7.78 t.

items.q: A coal deposit has reserves of 1,200 million tonnes. If 5 million tonnes are mined each year, how long will the reserves last?
items.e: Lifetime = reserves ÷ rate = 1,200 ÷ 5 = 240 years.

Wells made irrigated farming possible in an otherwise dry region.
Early farming villages grew along the Nile, Tigris and Euphrates rivers.
Farmers settle on the slopes of active volcanoes despite the danger.
items.e: Resources, hazards and climate shape where people live.
